title: Around every circle
hookLine: around every circle another can be drawn (Circles)

lines: THE FARTHEST THING YOU CAN SEE.
THE EYE IS THE FIRST CIRCLE.
cards: Look at the farthest thing you can see from where you are. A wall, a window, a line of rooftops, the edge of the sky. That edge is where your seeing stops.

Emerson's essay Circles starts right here, with the eye. "The eye is the first circle; the horizon which it forms is the second; and throughout nature this primary figure is repeated without end." Your pupil is a circle.
What it sees makes a bigger one, the horizon. And past that horizon, if you walk to it, is another.

teach.b: First, the central line: "Our life is an apprenticeship to the truth, that around every circle another can be drawn; that there is no end in nature, but every end is a beginning".

An apprenticeship: we're learning a trade, and the trade is this, no circle is the last one. Second, what that means for ideas. Every view we hold, Emerson says, is a circle we've drawn around our experience.
It feels like the edge of the world. Then a new thought comes, and the old circle is just a ring inside a bigger one.

teach.h: EVERY ULTIMATE FACT, A FIRST STEP.
teach.b: "Every ultimate fact is only the first of a new series." Third, what that means for people. Each person is drawing circles, Emerson says, and a life is a circle that keeps trying to widen.

He also notices how we resist: we get comfortable inside a circle and defend its edge, even against a better idea. Fourth, the link back. A few days ago, a foolish consistency: the freedom to change your mind.
Circles is the same freedom, seen as growth.
Changing isn't failing to hold a position; it's the next ring going out.

teach.h: AROUND EVERY CIRCLE ANOTHER CAN BE DRAWN.
teach.b: Yesterday's Over-Soul is here too: if each life is contained in something larger, there's always a larger circle still to draw. Emerson admits this is unsettling. Nothing stays fixed.
But for him that's the good news. Whatever looks like the limit today is, in his picture, one more circle.

how: Some readers take Emerson's Circles as a picture of growth: each view a person holds can be widened by the next one, and every end can be read as a beginning.

o: Emerson's idea that every limit can be widened again
a ring of friends who always support each other
a rule that a life should return to where it began

p: the first of a new series

s: the eye is the first circle; the horizon it forms is the second.
Emerson says our views are fixed edges of the world
each is a circle with another that can be drawn around it.
Emerson says the widening is always comfortable
he admits it's unsettling, and notices how we defend our edges.

games.q: a new idea comes along that doesn't fit inside the circle you've drawn. what does Emerson's essay point to?
o: defend the edge of your circle.
let the circle widen around the old one.
games.why: around every circle another can be drawn: the old view becomes a ring inside a bigger one, not a mistake to throw away.

practice: Pick one thing you feel sure you understand, a person you know well, your job, your neighborhood, a belief about yourself, and see the circle you've drawn around it, the edge where you stop looking.
Now gently draw one more circle outside it: what would someone standing a little further out see? Don't force an answer; just let the edge move outward one ring.

wordCard.voice: Around every circle. Emerson's line from Circles: around every circle another can be drawn, and every end is a beginning. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: another circle. Every end, in Emerson's picture, is also a beginning. Until tomorrow.
